3-minute-sensory-mindfulness-act.reason: Replace an inherited sensory-mindfulness article containing unsupported adherence claims, fixed weekly dose targets, invented internal observations and treatment-like expectations with a conservative present-moment awareness protocol grounded in current NHS mindfulness guidance. The public version presents sensory noticing as a mindfulness exercise that may help someone reconnect with the present moment, not as a guaranteed treatment or a precise three-to-five-minute dose.

lifeOsSource.whatYouDo: Pause somewhere safe and deliberately notice what is happening around you right now. Choose a few sights, sounds, textures, smells or tastes and describe them simply. When your attention drifts into planning, worry or commentary, notice that and gently return to one sensory detail.
lifeOsSource.checkIn: What did I notice, how easy or difficult was it to return attention to the present, and did this feel useful enough to try again?
lifeOsSource.reference: NHS Every Mind Matters — What is mindfulness?

faq.question: Does the practice need to last 3 to 5 minutes?
faq.answer: No. Three minutes can be a convenient boundary, but Brali does not treat it as an evidence-based dose. NHS mindfulness guidance includes very brief present-moment exercises such as taking a minute to notice the room around you.

faq.question: What if my mind keeps wandering?
faq.answer: That does not make the practice a failure. Notice where attention went and gently return to something you can see, hear, feel, smell or taste. The exercise is about returning attention to the present, not eliminating thought.

faq.question: Is this a treatment for anxiety or another mental-health condition?
faq.answer: No. Brali presents this as a general mindfulness exercise. NHS guidance notes that mindfulness may support mental wellbeing, but if anxiety, fear or another difficulty is affecting daily life or self-help is not enough, appropriate professional support is available.

intro.html: Mindfulness is about paying attention to what is happening in the present moment. NHS guidance suggests noticing the world around you, including shapes, colours, textures, sounds, smells and other sensations. Brali turns that into a small observation experiment. The goal is not to empty your mind or guarantee calm. It is simply to practise noticing what is here and returning attention when it drifts.

sections.title: 1. Choose a safe pause
sections.html: Use the exercise when you can safely give some attention to your surroundings. Do not do it while driving, crossing a road, operating machinery or doing another task that requires your full attention.

sections.title: 2. Notice a few sensory details
sections.html: Look around and choose a few concrete details. You might notice the colour and shape of an object, a sound in the room, the texture of clothing or a chair, a smell, or a taste. You do not need to use every sense or follow a fixed count.

sections.title: 3. Describe what is present
sections.html: Use simple descriptions such as warm, rough, quiet, bright or distant. The point is to contact the experience that is happening now rather than turning the exercise into analysis or a test of whether you are becoming calm enough.

sections.title: 4. Notice when attention wanders
sections.html: If you start planning, worrying or judging the exercise, simply notice that attention moved. NHS mindfulness guidance also suggests stepping back from thoughts and naming them. You can acknowledge the thought and return to one sensory detail.

sections.title: 5. Stop when the pause is enough
sections.html: There is no required three-minute, five-minute or weekly target. A short pause can be enough for the experiment. If continuing feels unhelpful or uncomfortable, stop and return to what you were doing.

sections.title: 6. Review your own signal
sections.html: In Brali, record what you noticed and whether returning attention to the present felt useful, neutral or difficult. Do not expect a prescribed reduction in stress or anxiety. If significant anxiety, fear or other mental-health difficulties are affecting daily life, use appropriate professional support rather than relying on this exercise alone.
